personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Tonks is established across OotP as a vivid, irreverent personality defined by several consistent traits: infectious enthusiasm and cheerfulness (she volunteers eagerly, exclaims 'Wotcher Harry!', entertains at dinner by morphing her nose), self-deprecating humor about her clumsiness and domestic incompetence ('I'm dead clumsy'), directness and informality (insisting on 'Tonks' over 'Nymphadora'), and physical expressiveness (her Metamorphmagus ability mirrors her emotional state as a literal visual cue). She is also sharp and situationally aware — she warns the Knight Bus conductor with menace ('If you shout his name I will curse you into oblivion'), argues confidently with Moody mid-flight, and engages substantively with Order intelligence. In HBP, her voice changes completely and deliberately: she becomes withdrawn, silent, mousy-haired, and emotionally hollow — a portrait of grief and survivor's guilt rendered with great specificity. In DH she is radiant again ('simply radiant') upon reconciliation with Lupin, and her final appearances show a woman of conviction and courage. The voice across all three books is consistently individuated — colloquial, energetic in health, visibly broken in grief, specific in diction ('Wotcher,' 'dead clumsy,' 'I owe Bellatrix').
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the films, Tonks's personality is present but severely compressed. In OotP (Film 1 in the corpus), she gets one exchange establishing her name aversion ('Don't call me Nymphadora') and one line of reassurance to Harry ('Don't worry, Harry, we'll explain everything'). The cheerfulness, clumsiness, self-deprecating humor, nose-morphing mealtime entertainment, and enthusiastic volunteerism that define her book personality in OotP are entirely absent from the film corpus. In HBP (Film 2 corpus), she appears briefly at a Christmas scene where she supports Harry's suspicion about Snape ('Perhaps Harry's right, Remus'), and leaves the Burrow — contextually suggesting her depression, though no mousy hair, no hollow expression, no explicit grief characterization appears in the film corpus text. In DH Part 1 (Film 3 corpus), she announces her pregnancy at Privet Drive ('My husband, the joker. By the way, wait until you hear the news! Remus and I are —') in a bright, warm moment, and praises Ron warmly ('Deserves that. Brilliant, he was'). At the wedding she whispers to Mrs. Weasley about her pregnancy with visible happiness. The theatrical Battle of Hogwarts scene (DH Part 2) has her only as a visual presence in the Great Hall — fingers intertwined with Lupin's in death. The scene of Tonks arriving at the Battle to fight beside Lupin is explicitly cut and excluded from scoring. The result is that the film preserves the broad markers of her personality (informal address, warmth, occasional directness) but eliminates the texture: the clumsiness comedy, the nose-morphing personality, the specific wit and irreverence, and critically, the entire HBP arc of depression and its distinctive voice.
personality_voice.difference: The most significant loss is the HBP personality register: the withdrawn, grey, emotionally devastated Tonks who speaks in flat monosyllables, avoids eye contact, and wanders the castle in misery. This is not a minor compression — it is the dominant characterization of Tonks across an entire book. The OotP personality is also flattened: the clumsiness jokes, dinner table morphing, mid-flight arguments with Moody, and volunteer enthusiasm are absent. What remains is a pleasant, warm background presence without the comic energy, specific voice, or emotional depth the books give her.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The book establishes two distinct and well-evidenced personality phases: vivid, clumsy, irreverent (OotP) and grief-hollowed, subdued, almost unrecognizable (HBP). The film preserves the first in outline only (name aversion survives, warmth survives) and eliminates the second almost entirely. The clumsiness — a defining physical-comedic trait across dozens of OotP scenes — has no film presence. The HBP voice transformation, explicitly described in the book as affecting her Metamorphmagus ability and speech patterns, is absent from the scored film corpus. This is not compression that preserves character; it is compression that removes defining traits. Score placed at 14 (character remains recognizable, important traits and tone reduced).

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Tonks serves multiple distinct narrative functions across the books. In OotP: she is an active escort and protector (she leads the broomstick formation, carries Harry's trunk, lures the Dursleys away with the fake lawn competition letter — an act of initiative and wit she personally devises), she is an informant about Ministry politics (explains Fudge's fear of Voldemort), she is a source of warmth and humor within Grimmauld Place, and she fights meaningfully at the Department of Mysteries (firing spells at Death Eaters, being felled by Bellatrix). In HBP: she is a mystery — her changed Patronus, her visits to Hogwarts, her emotional collapse — and functions as a living signal of how the war affects individuals personally. Her agency is real: she takes initiative in visiting Dumbledore, she engineers her own emotional confrontation with Lupin at Bill's bedside. In DH: she partners with Ron during the Seven Potters escape (her pair escapes Death Eaters and she praises Ron's Stunner), she is part of the Order's active resistance, and most critically she abandons her infant son to fight at the Battle of Hogwarts — an act of autonomous moral decision-making that costs her life. Her death is narratively significant precisely because she made that choice.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In OotP (film), Tonks's narrative role is reduced to a member of the rescue party with minimal individual function. She says 'Don't worry, Harry' and 'Don't call me Nymphadora' — her most significant OotP action, luring the Dursleys away, is absent. She plays no distinct role in the Department of Mysteries battle as captured in the film corpus. In HBP (film), she appears at the Christmas dinner briefly, supporting Harry's theory about Snape, and departs — no agency beyond a conversational contribution. In DH Part 1 (film), she announces her pregnancy, praises Ron's bravery after the Seven Potters escape, and appears at the wedding. Her most significant DH agency moment — the decision to leave Teddy and fight at Hogwarts — is explicitly a cut scene and cannot be credited. In DH Part 2 (film), she appears only as a corpse in the Great Hall with fingers intertwined with Lupin's. The agency of her final choice (leaving her infant to fight) is completely removed from the scored film.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The luring of the Dursleys (OotP agency) is absent. The Department of Mysteries fighting is not individually rendered in the film corpus. The HBP visits to Hogwarts and confrontation with Lupin are compressed to near-invisibility. The DH Battle of Hogwarts arrival — her most consequential autonomous act — is a cut scene. What remains is a supportive background presence who praises others (Ron), announces pregnancies, and dies offscreen.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Multiple specific acts of agency are absent or transferred: the Dursley ruse (her initiative), the Lupin confrontation at Bill's bedside (her emotional forcing of the relationship resolution), and the Battle of Hogwarts arrival (her moral choice). The golden rule applies: her most defining act of agency in DH — choosing to fight over staying with her child — is cut entirely. Her narrative function collapses from active protector, intelligence source, and moral agent to a peripheral Order member who dies between scenes. Score at 10 (role and agency clearly altered).

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Tonks's motivations are layered and evolve across the series. In OotP, she is driven by loyalty to Dumbledore and the Order, professional pride as an Auror, and genuine warmth toward Harry. In HBP, her motivations become dominated by two intersecting forces: survivor's guilt (she blames herself for Sirius's death because she failed to stop Bellatrix) and unrequited love for Lupin (she has fallen for him and he refuses the relationship on grounds of age, poverty, and werewolf status). These two motivations compound each other — she is depressed, her Metamorphmagus ability is failing, she is isolated. Her internal conflict is explicit: she wants Lupin to accept her love and acknowledge the relationship is not doomed by his condition. In DH, her motivation is reconciled (they marry) but a new conflict emerges: she must balance protection of her newborn son against her loyalty to the Order and her desire to fight. The corpus confirms she resolves this conflict by leaving Teddy with her mother to join the battle — a decision explicitly described as anguished ('I couldn't stand not knowing').
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: In the films, Tonks's survivor's guilt is entirely absent — there is no scene in the film corpus where this motivation is established or explored. Her love for Lupin is established obliquely in HBP (she appears at the Christmas dinner and there is clearly something between them) and confirmed in DH Part 1 (she announces their marriage and pregnancy). The tension of Lupin resisting the relationship — his stated reasons of being 'too old, too poor, too dangerous' — has some film presence in the HBP dinner scene context, but the depth and specificity of the internal conflict is not established. The DH conflict between motherhood and duty is cut (the Battle of Hogwarts arrival scene is excluded), so her final and most acute motivation — the anguished choice to fight — does not exist in the scored film.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Survivor's guilt is entirely absent. The specific texture of Lupin's resistance and Tonks's persistence across HBP is reduced to implication. The DH anguish of leaving Teddy is eliminated by the scene cut. What remains is a woman who loves Lupin, marries him, and has his baby — the motivational skeleton without the flesh of conflict.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The survivor's guilt motivation is not poorly explained — it is absent. This is a change, not a compression. The DH motivational conflict (mother vs. fighter) is eliminated entirely by the cut scene. The love-for-Lupin motivation survives in outline but without the internal conflict that gives it dramatic weight. Score at 8 (motivations partially altered and flattened).

character_arc.book_baseline: Tonks's arc across the books is clearly defined and spans three phases: (1) OotP — introduction as a vivid, clumsy, enthusiastic young Auror who is fully functional and joyful; (2) HBP — emotional collapse driven by survivor's guilt and unrequited love, manifesting in changed appearance, altered Patronus, withdrawal, and diminished Metamorphmagus ability; (3) DH — partial restoration via marriage and pregnancy, but culminating in the ultimate expression of her values: sacrificing her life by choosing to fight beside her husband rather than stay safe with her infant. The arc moves from vitality → grief → reconciled sacrifice. Key turning points are: Sirius's death (triggering the collapse), Lupin's acceptance at Bill's bedside (triggering restoration), and the decision to enter the Battle of Hogwarts (completing the arc with her death). The arc is complete and structurally deliberate.
character_arc.film_portrayal: In the films: Phase 1 (OotP) is present only as a sketch — Tonks is introduced as a young, friendly Auror, but the defining characterization that would make Phase 2 meaningful is absent. Phase 2 (HBP collapse) is almost entirely absent from the film corpus — her depression, changed Patronus, and emotional withdrawal are not depicted in any scored film scene. The HBP film has her briefly in the Christmas dinner scene appearing to support Harry, with no depiction of the grief arc. Phase 3 (DH reconciliation) is partially present — the pregnancy announcement and the wedding scene communicate happiness — but the culminating act of sacrifice that completes the arc is the cut Battle of Hogwarts arrival scene. She dies in the film, but the arc that gives her death meaning — the conscious choice to leave her child — is removed.
character_arc.difference: The entire middle phase of the arc (HBP grief) is missing. The culminating act of the arc (DH choice to fight) is cut. What remains is introduction and death, without the transformation that connects them. The arc cannot be described as compressed — it is structurally absent.
character_arc.penalty_logic: A character arc requires its turning points to exist. The HBP phase is the emotional core of Tonks's arc — it is what makes her DH happiness meaningful and her death devastating. Its absence means the films portray a character who is introduced, marries, has a baby, and dies, without any of the internal journey that the books construct. The cut Battle of Hogwarts scene removes the arc's final beat. Score at 7 (arc significantly altered — the middle phase is missing and the culminating beat is cut).

key_relationships.book_baseline: Tonks's two most important relationships are: (1) Tonks and Lupin — the central emotional relationship of her arc, defined by her persistent love, his guilt-driven resistance, their eventual reconciliation, marriage, and joint death; it is the relationship that drives her HBP depression, changes her Patronus, and gives her DH arc its meaning. (2) Tonks and the Order (especially Mad-Eye Moody) — Mad-Eye is described as her mentor and the person who trained her, she is his 'favourite and his protégée at the Ministry.' Her grief at his death is singled out as specific and personal. Secondary: her relationship with Sirius (distant cousins, she cares about him and feels guilt for his death) and her relationship with Harry (warm, slightly teasing, genuinely protective).
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Tonks-Lupin relationship exists in the films but is dramatically compressed. The tension and resistance that defines HBP — Lupin's stated reasons, Tonks's seizing of his robes and shaking him, the public confrontation witnessed by Harry, Mrs. Weasley, and Mr. Weasley — is entirely absent from the scored film corpus. The film establishes their marriage and pregnancy but skips the conflict that made the relationship dramatically textured. Their shared death (fingers intertwined) is an emotionally resonant image in the film, but it is the conclusion of a relationship that was never fully dramatized. The Tonks-Moody relationship is not present at all in the scored film scenes — her grief at his death, her being his protégée, are not depicted. The Tonks-Harry relationship is present but minimal (one reassuring line in OotP, one rescue at the train station in HBP which is not in the film corpus).
key_relationships.difference: The Tonks-Lupin relationship survives as a fact (they are married, she loves him) but the emotional dynamic — specifically the conflict, her persistence, and his resistance — is absent. The Tonks-Moody mentorship relationship is entirely absent from the scored film. The grief at Sirius that drives her HBP characterization is absent.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The relationship that defines Tonks's character across HBP and DH (Lupin) is present in outline but its dynamic is removed. The secondary relationship that defines a key emotional beat in DH (Moody as mentor) is absent entirely. Per the scoring rubric, penalizing because the emotional dynamic and function of these relationships is altered or absent, not simply because there are fewer scenes. Score at 5 (important relationship dynamics altered or weakened).

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Tonks's book complexity rests on several interlocking elements: (1) The comedic-physical texture of clumsiness and Metamorphmagus play that makes her charming and individuated in OotP; (2) The counterintuitive HBP portrait of a skilled Auror reduced to emotional wreckage — contradicting her OotP competence and revealing the cost of war on individuals; (3) The specificity of her survivor's guilt (not general grief but the specific belief that she should have stopped Bellatrix); (4) The Patronus as a living symbol of internal state — its transformation to a werewolf shape is one of the book's subtler pieces of characterization; (5) The DH tension between her role as new mother and her identity as a fighter; (6) Her relationship with her family background (half-blood, Andromeda's daughter, Black family tapestry connection); (7) Her death as the consequence of a deliberate moral choice, not random battle casualty. These layers make her a character who is simultaneously comic, tragic, professional, in love, politically embedded, and morally purposeful.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve: her name, her Auror status, her love for Lupin, her pregnancy, her death in battle. They eliminate: the entire clumsiness comedy texture of OotP, the HBP grief arc and its specific cause, the Patronus symbolism (never depicted in film as a changed werewolf shape), the Moody mentorship, the survivor's guilt, the Black family connection, and the DH choice to fight over staying with Teddy. The image of Tonks and Lupin with intertwined fingers is genuinely moving but it is the residue of complexity rather than complexity itself — the audience cannot know what it costs her unless the prior characterization exists.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films retain Tonks's identity and broad function (Order member, Lupin's wife) while removing most of what makes her a fully realized individual. The comedy texture of OotP, the tragedy texture of HBP, and the moral texture of DH are all substantially absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The simplification is major. The surviving film portrayal reduces Tonks to: warm, married-to-Lupin, dies in battle. This is the outline of the character without her substance. The HBP arc — arguably the most complex portrayal of how war damages an individual in the entire series, told through a secondary character — is absent. The DH moral choice is cut. The OotP personality texture is present only in trace form. Score at 7 (major flattening; character reduced to simpler function). Cap rule 1 applies: a major part of complexity, agency, and narrative function is removed.

comparative.key_observations: Tonks is one of the most substantially altered major supporting characters in the adaptation. The films preserve her identity — her name, her Auror status, her love for Lupin, her marriage, her pregnancy, her death — but almost entirely remove the characterization that makes her interesting: the vivid, clumsy, irreverent OotP personality; the devastating HBP grief arc driven by survivor's guilt and unrequited love; the Patronus symbolism; her mentor relationship with Moody; and critically, her final act of autonomous moral agency — leaving her newborn son to fight beside her husband. Her death in the film is visually poignant (fingers intertwined with Lupin's) but narratively hollow because the arc that would make it devastating has not been built. The film portrayal is recognizable but not faithful: it is the skeleton of a character rather than the character herself.
